warmup.q: The card payments program can answer 1,000 payments a second, and 800 arrive each second. Something it depends on slows down for five seconds, and a line of waiting payments builds up. Card readers give up on any answer that takes longer than 200 ms and send the payment again, up to 4 times in all. Then the slow part recovers fully. What happens next?
options: It recovers within a second or two, as soon as the line empties
It recovers after about as long as the slowdown lasted
It stays overloaded: the repeated sends keep the load above what it can answer, until someone cuts the load or the repeats
It crashes at once and starts again cleanly
warmup.why: Once every attempt takes too long, each payment turns into four attempts. So the program is sent several times what it can answer, even after the slow part is fine, and it spends its time answering card readers that already gave up. In this lesson's simulation it never recovers. The first two answers assume the line empties once the program is back to full speed. That only happens if less work arrives than it can do, and the repeats prevent exactly that. The fourth section builds this up.

sections.h: A part breaks, but does the service? Faults and failures
sections.html:
At 03:12 one night, a disk dies in the computer that runs the payments database, the program that stores every payment. (A disk is the part of a computer that keeps data when the power is off.) What happened to the payments business?

It depends on what else was there. Suppose the database kept a copy of its data on a second computer and switched to it within seconds. Then no card reader noticed. Suppose instead that this disk held the only copy. Then no card payment has worked since 03:12, and the last few payments may be gone. The disk broke either way. What differs is whether the service did.

Two words keep this straight. A fault is one part not working as it should: a disk, a computer, a network cable, a bug in one function, or a slow program it depends on. A failure is the whole system no longer giving its users the service it promised. Lesson 2 made that promise exact as a target, the SLO: say, 99.9% of payments answered well over 30 days. In any system of real size, faults happen all the time. Being reliable means working correctly while some parts are faulty, and a system that does is fault-tolerant.

Fault tolerance always has limits. A design survives particular faults, up to some number: any one disk, any one computer, or one availability zone. (Cloud companies, which rent out computers, keep them in regions near big cities. Each region has a few availability zones, separate buildings with their own power and network.) Nothing survives everything. A bug in every copy of the code defeats any amount of spare hardware. So the useful question about a design is: which faults, and how many?

A part whose fault alone becomes a failure of the whole system is a single point of failure. It might be the one database with no copy, or the one load balancer, the machine at the front door that hands requests to the copies of the program. It might even be the one person who knows how to rerun the nightly job that pays the shops.

A design survives the faults it names, and no others. Name them.

Two kinds of failure aren't equal. An outage, an hour when nobody can pay, is costly and embarrassing, and then it's over. A payment that was accepted and then lost, or a balance that is quietly wrong, doesn't get better with time. The UK Post Office's Horizon accounting software is the sad example. From 1999 it reported missing money in branch accounts that wasn't missing. Hundreds of people who ran local post offices were convicted of theft or false accounting on its evidence, partly because the courts presumed the computer was right. So most data systems would rather refuse a payment than accept it and lose it.

We'll take the kinds of fault in turn: hardware, software, and people changing things. Hardware comes first, because it can be counted.

try.title: Find the single points of failure
steps: Here is the payments company's setup. Two computers run the payments program, behind one load balancer. One PostgreSQL database (a popular free database program) keeps the payments. A second copy of it, updated as each payment arrives, sits in the same rack, a metal cabinet of computers that share one power supply. A Redis cache (Redis is a program that keeps data in memory) holds each shop's balance. A nightly job that pays the shops runs on one computer, started by a schedule that only one engineer knows how to fix. And both payment computers read the password for the card banks from one file on a shared network drive.
For each part, ask: if this alone breaks, do card payments stop? Do the shops still get paid?
Sort the parts into single points of failure and faults the design tolerates. For each tolerated fault, write down what has to be true for it really to be tolerated.
try.expect:
The single points of failure, the parts whose fault alone stops card payments:

  • The one load balancer in front of the two payment computers.
  • The shared network drive. If it's unavailable, neither computer can read the bank password, so both fail together. One shared part undoes the spare.
  • The rack. The database and its copy sit in one rack, so one power fault takes out both.
  • For paying the shops, the one computer and the one engineer who knows the schedule. Card payments keep working, but the shops don't get paid.

Faults the design tolerates: either payment computer; the database's disk or computer, if switching to the copy works and has been tested; and Redis, as long as the code treats an empty or missing cache as "read from the database". Redis holds derived data (What a data system is), so losing it costs speed, not facts. If you marked Redis as a single point of failure, check how the code behaves when it's down: that's what decides.

sections.h: Disks, memory and processors: rare faults for one, routine for thousands
sections.html:
Hardware faults have one big advantage: they can be counted. Every three months, Backblaze, a company that stores other people's files, publishes how often its hard drives fail. (Hard drives are the most common kind of disk.) Its measure is the annualized failure rate (AFR): the share of drives that fail in a year. Across 344,196 drives in 2025, the AFR was 1.36%. In the second quarter of 2026 (April to June) it was 1.73%. The worst models that quarter were seven to eight and a half years old, and failed at 7% to 9% a year. Old drives fail more.

1.36% sounds small until you multiply it. A computer with 12 disks has a 15% chance of losing at least one this year. A fleet of 10,000 disks (a fleet is all the disks or computers a company runs) loses about 136 a year, one every two or three days. At this scale a dead disk is a routine chore, like changing a light bulb, and the software has to treat it that way.

Memory next. A computer's memory is its fast working storage, wiped when the power goes, and it holds everything as bits, ones and zeros. A 2009 study of Google's computers found that about a third of them saw at least one memory error a year that could be corrected. ECC memory (error-correcting code) stores a few extra bits with the data, so the hardware can spot a flipped bit and repair it. But 1.3% of computers a year hit an error that ECC can spot and can't repair, and the computer crashes or stops. Then processors, the chips that run a program's instructions. Meta, Google and Alibaba have each reported that about 1 in 1,000 of their processors can compute wrong results without any error. That's silent data corruption: no crash and no message, only a wrong number in someone's balance.

The defence against hardware faults is redundancy: more than one copy, on more than one disk. Data on one disk is lost with the disk, 1.37% a year. With a second copy on another disk, it's lost only if the second disk dies before the first one's copy has been re-created. With a 24-hour repair, that's about 1 in a million a year, and a third copy makes it about 6 in 100 billion. The figure shows the race. Each extra copy multiplies safety by roughly the chance of a failure inside one repair window. So a quick repair matters as much as the number of copies: a week-long repair makes a pair seven times riskier than a one-day repair.

Keep copies apart, and repair them fast.

All of this assumes disks fail independently, each for its own reasons. They don't, quite. Drives from one factory batch share defects, and one rack's power supply takes down every disk in it. (A rack is a metal cabinet of computers.) So real systems put copies in different racks and zones.

Hardware faults mostly strike one part at a time, which is why copies work. Next, we'll meet faults that strike every copy at once.

The data is lost only if disk B fails inside that window."><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t" x="20" y="77" text-anchor="start">disk A</text><text class="t" x="20" y="147" text-anchor="start">disk B</text><rect class="box" x="100" y="60" width="200" height="24" rx="4"/><text class="t-s" x="200" y="77" text-anchor="middle">copy 1</text><rect class="box-bad" x="300" y="60" width="40" height="24" rx="4"/><rect class="box" x="340" y="60" width="280" height="24" rx="4"/><text class="t-s" x="480" y="77" text-anchor="middle">re-created copy</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="320" y="48" text-anchor="middle">A fails: 24 h to re-create its copy</text><line class="ln-d" x1="300" y1="88" x2="300" y2="122"/><line class="ln-d" x1="340" y1="88" x2="340" y2="122"/><rect class="box" x="100" y="130" width="520" height="24" rx="4"/><text class="t-s" x="200" y="147" text-anchor="middle">copy 2</text><rect class="box-b" x="296" y="124" width="48" height="36" rx="4"/><text class="t-s t-b" x="320" y="180" text-anchor="middle">data is lost only if B also fails inside this window</text><line class="ln" x1="100" y1="200" x2="620" y2="200"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="100" y="218" text-anchor="start">1 January</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="620" y="218" text-anchor="end">31 December</text></svg>

try.title: Count disk failures and lost data
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It prints how many disk failures to expect for three fleet sizes, the yearly chance of losing data kept on 1, 2 or 3 disks, and a simulation that checks the formula.

Predict before it prints. 10,000 disks are set up as 5,000 mirrored pairs, each disk a mirror copy of its partner, with a one-day repair. Is the yearly chance that some pair loses its data closer to 1 in a million, 1 in 200, or 1 in 2?
Change AFR to 0.08 (drives in their eighth year) in DiskOddsDemo.kt and run it again. Which line changes most?

code.title: DiskOddsDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: private fun lossPerYear(copies: Int, afr: Double, repair: Double) = copies * ratePerHour(afr).pow(copies) * repair.pow(copies - 1) * HOURS_PER_YEAR // and a Monte Carlo check: disks fail at random, come back `repair` hours later; // count the moments when every copy is down at once

try.expect:
AFR 1.36%, repair 24 h
     12 disks:    0.2 failures a year expected, chance of at least one: 15.2%
  1,000 disks:   13.6 failures a year expected, chance of at least one: 100.0%
 10,000 disks:  136.0 failures a year expected, chance of at least one: 100.0%

one piece of data on N disks, chance per year of losing every copy:
  1 copy : 1.37e-02
  2 copies: 1.03e-06
  3 copies: 5.78e-11
10,000 disks as 5,000 mirrored pairs: chance some pair loses its data this year: 0.51%
same pairs, repair takes a week instead of a day: 3.53%

check: 2 copies, 1 failure per 1,000 h, 10 h repair, 2e+07 hours: formula 400 losses, simulation 385

With 1,000 disks, a failure this year is certain (the chance prints as 100.0%, rounded). Copies change the picture. In the output, 1.03e-06 means 1.03 millionths, about one in a million, so at this failure rate and repair time each extra copy makes losing one piece of data more than 10,000 times rarer. A fleet of 5,000 mirrored pairs still has about one chance in 200 a year that some pair loses its data, and a slow repair makes it seven times worse. The last line checks the formula against a simulation at deliberately high failure rates, and they agree within the simulation's noise.

With AFR = 0.08 the risk for each pair becomes 3.81e-05, and the fleet line jumps from 0.51% to 17.34% a year (73.65% with a week-long repair). A pair squares the failure rate, so drives that fail 6 times as often make losing a pair about 37 times as likely. That's why old drives get replaced before they die.

refs.title: Schroeder, Pinheiro and Weber, DRAM Errors in the Wild (SIGMETRICS 2009)

sections.h: One bug, every machine: software faults and health checks that lie
sections.html:
A disk fails on one computer. A bug fails on every computer that runs the code, often at the same moment, because they all run the same code on the same inputs. Redundancy, which saved us from the disk, now copies the damage.

In 2025, three companies whose systems many others rely on had famous examples:

  • Google Cloud, 12 June: a settings change with blank fields was written to a database that copies itself worldwide, and it reached every region within seconds. Code added two weeks earlier read those settings without checking them, and crashed on the blanks, everywhere.
  • Amazon Web Services (AWS), 19 and 20 October: two parts of an automatic tool acted at once, in an order nobody had planned for, which is called a race. It left DynamoDB, Amazon's database service, with no address in its Virginia region. Errors lasted about three hours, and some services built on it took far longer to recover.
  • Cloudflare, a company whose network sits in front of millions of websites, 18 November: a change to database permissions made a database question, a query, return every result twice. The settings file it built for spotting robots grew past a size limit in Cloudflare's software, which failed across its network as the file spread.

One pattern runs through them. Data or settings that were accepted as valid reached every machine at once, and hit code that had never seen that case. Roll changes out in stages, so a bad one hits a few machines first. Have every program check what it receives, such as sizes and missing fields, and keep the last good version when the new one is bad. Put new code behind a feature flag, a switch that turns it off without installing a new version.

Error handling is where much of this hides. Ding Yuan and colleagues studied 198 failures that users reported in widely used data systems (OSDI, a research conference, 2014). In 92% of the worst ones, the cause was the error handler, the code that runs when something goes wrong, mishandling an error the software had already noticed. Many were trivial: an empty catch block, a handler that only logged, a TODO left in place. In 58% of them, a simple test that made the error handler run would have found the bug. The Try it shows this in the nightly job that pays the shops.

The hardest software faults crash nothing. A gray failure is one where a part looks healthy to whatever checks it, while its users see it broken. Microsoft's cloud team reported in 2017 that gray failures, not clean crashes, were behind most of its incidents. In one, a bug broke the network of a virtual machine, one of many pretend computers sharing a real one. Its heartbeats, regular "I'm alive" messages, travelled by a separate path. So the health checks, the automatic tests that ask each part whether it's working, stayed green until a customer complained.

Check health the way users see it, through the real path.

Some faults clear up on their own, and the usual answer to those is to try again. Next, we'll see how trying again can keep a program down.

try.title: Run three error handlers against one fault
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. A nightly job sends five payout instructions (orders to pay a shop) to a pretend bank. The upload for the shop m-bikes fails once in the first three runs, and every time in the last.
Before it prints, predict what each version reports, and how many payouts the bank really received.
Look at the excerpt. If you had to write one test that would have caught the first version, what would it do?

code.title: ErrorHandlerDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: try { bank.upload(m, c) } catch (e: IOException) { // TODO: retry }

try.expect:
-- swallow the exception, one dropped connection
    reports: job finished: OK
    the bank received 4 of 5 payouts
-- log and continue, one dropped connection
    warn: upload for m-bikes failed: connection reset by peer
    reports: job finished: OK (1 warnings)
    the bank received 4 of 5 payouts
-- retry, then fail the job, one dropped connection
    reports: job finished: OK
    the bank received 5 of 5 payouts
-- retry, then fail the job, bank keeps failing
    reports: job FAILED: no payout for [m-bikes], settlement blocked
    the bank received 4 of 5 payouts

The first two versions turn a dropped connection into a shop that doesn't get paid, and report success. The second at least logs a warning, which nobody is alerted about. The third retries, which fixes a fault that passes. When the fault doesn't go away, it fails the job loudly, so a person finds out tonight, not when m-bikes calls. A test that makes bank.upload throw and expects the job to fail would have caught the first version.

One condition hides in the retry. It's only safe because sending the same payout instruction twice must not pay twice. Real payout files carry an instruction number that the bank uses to drop repeats, the idempotency key from Latency, percentiles and the tail.

refs.title: Yuan et al., Simple Testing Can Prevent Most Critical Failures (OSDI 2014)
Huang et al., Gray Failure: The Achilles' Heel of Cloud-Scale Systems (HotOS 2017)

aside.title: Doesn't a backup protect against bad data?
aside.html: Only if the bad data can't reach it. Copies that update themselves as data arrives copy the bad write too, within seconds. A backup taken before the bug can bring the good data back, as long as the bug couldn't overwrite or delete it. That's why careful teams keep some backups that nothing can change for a while, and practise restoring them. Until you've restored a backup once, you don't know that it works.

sections.h: Retry storms: when trying again keeps the outage going
sections.html:
Trying a failed request again, a retry, is the obvious answer to a fault, and usually the right one: the dropped connection in the last Try it needed exactly one. Under overload, though, the same retries can keep a program down after the cause has gone.

A coffee counter shows how. The barista makes drinks in the order the slips sit on the rail. A customer who has waited three minutes gives up, goes back to the till and orders again, leaving the first slip on the rail. Then the coffee machine runs slowly for a few minutes. Slips pile up, people reorder, and soon the barista is making drinks for people who have left. In programming terms, the barista is the server, the program doing the work. The rail is the queue, the three minutes are the timeout (how long a client waits before giving up), and reordering is a retry.

Now with numbers. A program can finish 1,000 requests a second and gets 800, so it's 80% busy and answers in about a millisecond. Its clients, the programs sending it requests, give up on an attempt after 200 ms and try again at once, up to 4 attempts in all. At t = 10 s (ten seconds into the run), something it depends on slows down. For five seconds it can finish only 400 a second. The stepper follows the lab's simulation.

The trigger doesn't last. By t = 15 s the program can finish 1,000 a second again. But it now gets 3,200 attempts a second, because every request times out and is sent four times. And it spends all its effort on attempts whose clients gave up long ago. Goodput, the rate of answers someone is still waiting for, is zero, and it stays zero for the rest of the run.

This is a metastable failure, the name Nathan Bronson and colleagues gave it in 2021. A trigger pushes the system into a bad state, and its own behaviour keeps it there after the trigger is gone. Getting out needs a strong push, such as cutting the load or restarting. Lexiang Huang and colleagues studied 22 such failures at 11 organizations (OSDI 2022). At least 4 of 15 major AWS outages in the previous ten years were metastable, and retries were the most common thing keeping them going.

The lab compares fixes on the same trigger:

Clients and server Back to normal at
retry up to 4 attempts at once never
exponential backoff with jitter, 4 attempts never
no retries at all t = 24 s
retries limited by a 10% budget t = 34 s
retry up to 4, and the server drops expired attempts t = 15 s

Backoff waits longer before each retry, usually doubling the wait each time (exponential backoff), with a random part called jitter so that clients don't retry in step. It spreads retries out in time, but here every attempt still times out, so there are as many. A retry budget caps their number: retries may add at most 10% to the work coming in. Then the program never gets more than 880 a second. It works off its backlog, the work piled up in the line, but slowly, because it still spends effort on attempts nobody is waiting for. Dropping those fixes the rest. Each request carries its deadline, and the server drops attempts whose deadline has passed without working on them, like a barista who bins slips older than three minutes. Then every bit of effort goes to a request that can still succeed.

Give retries a budget, and drop work nobody waits for.

The coffee counter breaks in one place: a real customer reorders once and goes home, while a program retries four times and never tires. Next, we'll look at what started most of this lesson's incidents: a change someone made.

stepper.title: A five-second slowdown that never ends
stepper.intro: The lab's simulation, one moment at a time. Goodput counts the answers that reach a client still waiting for them.

During the trigger all 400 answers a second are useful. The moment the program is back to full speed, so is the service, and it clears the backlog with 880 good answers in the next second.

try.title: Tip a service into a retry storm
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It runs the same five-second trigger with five different retry rules, and prints a few seconds of each run.
Predict before you look: which runs are back to normal by t = 40 s?
Add -Pargs=backoff to run only the backoff rule. Compare its attempts per second with plain retries. What did backoff change, and what didn't it?

code.title: RetryStormDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: // a timed-out attempt is sent again (if the policy allows) if (policy.allowRetry(a.number)) send(a.request, a.number + 1, now) // the server works on the oldest attempt, whether or not anyone still waits for it val a = queue.pollFirst() if (config.shedExpired && now > a.deadline) continue // the fix: drop it unread capAcc -= 1.0 if (now <= a.deadline && a.request !in done) { done += a.request; goodput++ } else wasted++

try.expect:
-- retry up to 4 attempts: recovered at never
   t   new  attempts  goodput  wasted  queued
   5   800       800      800       0       0
  10   800      1757      161     239    1357
  11   800      3200        0     400    4157
  15   800      3200        0    1000   14757
  20   800      3200        0    1000   25757
  59   800      3200        0    1000  111557
-- retry budget, 10%: recovered at t=34s
   t   new  attempts  goodput  wasted  queued
  11   800       880        0     400     937
  15   800       880        0    1000    2257
  30   800       880        0    1000     457
  40   800       800      800       0       0
-- retry up to 4, server sheds expired work: recovered at t=15s
   t   new  attempts  goodput  wasted  queued
  11   800      2000      400       0     404
  15   800       978     1000       0      80
  16   800       800      880       0       0

(output trimmed to a few rows per run). In the columns, new is fresh requests per second, attempts counts those plus retries, wasted is answers nobody was waiting for, and queued is the length of the line. With plain retries, goodput drops to zero within a second of the trigger and never comes back. The budget holds attempts at 880 a second, below what the program can do, but the server still wastes its time on a backlog of expired attempts until about t = 34 s. Dropping expired work keeps every answer useful: 400 good answers a second during the trigger (all the program can do then), and full service from t = 15 s, even though the clients still retry four times. The simulation runs the same way every time, so you get these numbers exactly.

With -Pargs=backoff the attempts per second wobble towards 3,200 (1,438, then 3,063, then 3,228 in seconds 10 to 12) instead of jumping straight there. The jitter spread the retries out; it didn't remove any, and the run never recovers.

sections.h: Most outages start with a change: people, post-mortems and practice
sections.html:
Look back at this lesson's incidents: in most of them, something changed. A new version went out, or a settings file was sent to every machine. The largest single cause of outages is people changing a running system.

The best-known example is Amazon S3, Amazon's service for storing files, on 28 February 2017. An engineer, following an established checklist, ran a command to take a few computers out of a part of the system used for billing, and mistyped one input. The command removed far more computers than intended, including computers of two parts that every S3 request in that region depended on. Both had to restart completely. Neither had been fully restarted there for many years, so the restarts were slow. S3 in that region was down for about four hours, and so were many services built on it.

David Oppenheimer and colleagues (2003) found that changes to settings, made by the people running the systems, were the leading cause of outages in the internet services they studied. Hardware was a cause in only 10% to 25%. Google's book on keeping large systems running, Site Reliability Engineering, says roughly 70% of its outages come from changes to a live system. Its answer is to roll changes out step by step, notice problems fast and make every change easy to undo.

It's tempting to write "human error" in the incident report and stop there. Don't. The engineer did what the tool allowed, following the written procedure. The useful questions are about the system: why could one typo remove that much? AWS's fixes changed the system. The tool now removes computers slowly and refuses to go below a safe minimum. And the part that was slowest to restart is being split into smaller pieces.

Human error is where the search starts. Keep asking what the system allowed.

Two habits make teams better at this over time. A post-mortem is a written record of an incident: what happened and when, the harm, the causes, and the actions that will stop it happening again. A blameless one assumes that everyone acted reasonably with what they knew at the time. People who expect blame hide what they did, and then nobody learns why the system let it happen.

Chaos engineering tests fault tolerance on purpose. Say what normal looks like (for example, the share of card payments that succeed), predict that it will hold, break something real, and look for a difference. You might switch off a computer, block messages to a program the system depends on, or fill a disk. Netflix, the film-streaming company, built the best-known tool, Chaos Monkey, which switches off its own computers at random while customers are using them. Both habits rest on Yuan's finding from the third section: recovery code that never runs probably doesn't work. So make it run, on your schedule, and not at 03:12.

try.title: Make three post-mortem lines blameless
steps: Rewrite each line so it says what the system allowed, instead of who slipped. Invent the details you need.
1. "A developer ran the database change against the live system by mistake." 2. "The engineer on duty that night was slow to respond." 3. "The testers didn't test the error handler."
For each, write one action that changes a tool, an alert or a test.
try.expect:
Model rewrites (yours will differ in the details you invent; the shape is what matters):

  1. "The script that changes the database reads its target from a setting, which was pointing at the live database in the window it ran from. Nothing asked for confirmation before it ran against the live system." Action: the script refuses to run against the live database without an extra option, and prints its target before it starts.
  2. "The first alert went to a group chat at 02:10. The alert that wakes the engineer on duty went out at 02:31, when the error rate crossed a second threshold." Action: wake the engineer based on the burn rate of the payments target (Latency, percentiles and the tail), not on a fixed error rate.
  3. "No test made the upload's error branch run, so the empty handler had never been executed." Action: a test that makes the upload fail and expects the job to fail.

Each rewrite says what the system allowed, and each action changes a tool, an alert or a test, never "be more careful".

opening:
Picture the café on a busy morning. The card reader on the counter stops working, so the owner takes the spare from a drawer and plugs it in. The queue barely notices. One part broke, and the café kept taking payments.

A week later, every card reader in town stops at the same moment. The spares don't help, because the readers are fine. The fault is in the program they all talk to, and a new version of it went live that morning.

It's tempting to think that spares make you safe. They do protect against the common kind of break, which is why they're so convincing. Lesson 2, Latency, percentiles and the tail, ended with a promise about how often payments may fail. In this lesson, we'll tell a part breaking from the service breaking, and count what spares buy. Then we'll see why one bug defeats every spare, watch retries keep a program down, and look at the people who make changes. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two broken card readers. The spare in the drawer covered the first, because one part broke. Nothing covered the second, because one change broke every reader at once. Copies protect against faults that strike one part at a time. Careful changes, limited retries and honest post-mortems protect against the rest.

Next time an app you use goes down, look afterwards for the company's status page, where many companies report outages and their causes. Find the first change that started it, and ask what the system allowed.

Next, we'll measure how much work a system has to carry, and find out why the average user is never the one who breaks it.

compare.title: Plain retries and budgeted retries

a.label: Plain retries
a.title: a common default
a.html: // up to 4 attempts, straight away fun <T> withRetries(call: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(4) { try { return call() } catch (e: TimeoutException) { last = e } } throw last!! }

b.label: A retry budget
b.title: at most 10% extra load
b.html: // retries may add at most 10% load, spaced out with backoff and jitter class RetryBudget(private val ratio: Double = 0.1, private val max: Double = 10.0) { private var tokens = 0.0 @Synchronized fun onRequest() { tokens = minOf(max, tokens + ratio) } @Synchronized fun tryRetry(): Boolean = (tokens >= 1.0).also { if (it) tokens -= 1.0 } } fun <T> withBudget(budget: RetryBudget, call: () -> T): T { budget.onRequest() var attempt = 0 while (true) { try { return call() } catch (e: TimeoutException) { if (++attempt == 4 || !budget.tryRetry()) throw e Thread.sleep(Random.nextLong(0, minOf(2_000L, 50L shl attempt))) // full jitter } } }

compare.note: On a normal day the two behave the same: a rare timeout is retried, and the retry works. On a bad day the first sends four times the traffic to a program that is already struggling. The second lets each request earn a tenth of a retry, like a coin dropped in a jar, and each retry spends a whole coin. So however bad things get, retries add at most about 10% to the load. It also waits a random time before each retry it allows (full jitter), so clients don't retry in step. @Synchronized makes the two functions take turns when several threads call them at once. The lab builds the same budget for the simulation.

worked.title: How likely is it to lose data kept on two disks?

steps.say: Turn the yearly failure rate into a rate per hour, written λ (the Greek letter lambda). For small AFRs this is almost exactly AFR / 8,760, the number of hours in a year.
steps.code: λ = -ln(1 - 0.0136) / 8,760 hours = 1.563e-6 failures per disk per hour

steps.say: A pair of disks loses its data when one disk fails (2 × λ per hour, because either can go first) and the other fails before the 24-hour repair is done (about λ × 24). Call the repair time R.
steps.code:
loss rate = 2 × λ × (λ × R)
          = 2 × 1.563e-6 × (1.563e-6 × 24)
          = 1.17e-10 per hour
          × 8,760 hours = 1.03e-6 per year   (about 1 in a million)

steps.say: Scale up to the fleet: 10,000 disks as 5,000 independent pairs. Work out the chance that at least one pair loses its data this year.

Change one input at a time to see what matters. The repair time appears once, so a week instead of a day multiplies the risk by 7. A third copy multiplies it by about 1.5 × λ × R, roughly 1 in 18,000.
steps.code:
repair 168 h:  7.19e-6 per pair, 3.5% for the fleet
three copies:  3 × λ³ × R² × 8,760 = 5.78e-11 per year

steps.say: Remember what the formula assumes: failures that are independent. Two disks from one batch, or in one rack on one power supply, fail together far more often than this. That's why copies go to different racks and zones.
steps.code:
assumption: disk failures are independent
reality:    same batch, same rack, same firmware bug -> correlated

lab.title: Tip a service into a retry storm, then pull it out
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. 14 tests run and 10 fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's way of saying a function's body is still a TODO. Four pass already: they run the finished simulator with retry rules that are already written, and show the storm itself.
Read simulateStorm in RetryStorm.kt. Find the two lines that make the storm: where a timed-out attempt is sent again, and where the server works on an attempt whose deadline has passed.

Write RetryBudget.onRequest and allowRetry. The budget is a jar of tokens: each new request adds a tenth of a token, and each retry spends a whole one. Run RetryStormTest. With your budget the service should be back by t = 40 s, and no second should see more attempts than 110% of new requests plus the 10 tokens the jar can hold.
In DiskOdds.kt, write the four functions. The KDoc above each one (the comment that documents it) gives the formula, and ratePerHour is done.
Run all the tests until they pass. The last test in DiskOddsTest checks your formula against a simulation of disks failing and being re-created.
hints: allowRetry: return false when attempt >= maxAttempts or tokens < 1.0; otherwise subtract 1.0 and return true. Check before you spend.
lossChancePerYear: with val lambda = ratePerHour(afr), return copies * lambda.pow(copies) * repairHours.pow(copies - 1) * HOURS_PER_YEAR.

drill.title: The storm and the odds, from memory
drill.prompt: Without notes: (1) say what a metastable failure is, in one sentence; (2) say why backoff alone didn't save the program in the lab; (3) name the two fixes that did; (4) give the expected yearly disk failures for 10,000 disks at 1.36% AFR, and the formula for the yearly chance of losing data kept on a pair of disks.

answer.html:
(1) A trigger pushes the system into a bad state, and its own behaviour
    (here, retries) keeps it there after the trigger is gone.
(2) Backoff spreads the retries out in time, but every attempt still times out,
    so each request still becomes 4 attempts: 3,200 a second against 1,000.
(3) A retry budget (retries add at most ~10% load), and the server dropping
    attempts whose deadline has passed, so capacity only goes to live requests.
(4) 10,000 x 0.0136 = 136 a year, one every 2 to 3 days.
    Pair: 2 x λ x (λ x R) per hour x 8,760, with λ = AFR / 8,760 (about)
    and R the repair time in hours: about 1 in a million for a 24 h repair.

recap: A fault is one part going wrong; a failure is the service missing its promise. A fault-tolerant design names the faults it survives, and how many.
Hardware faults are routine at scale (10,000 disks at 1.36% AFR lose one every two or three days) and mostly independent. Copies in different places, plus a fast repair, make data loss very rare.
Software and settings faults strike every machine at once, so copies don't help. Roll changes out in stages, check what each program receives, and test the error handlers.
Retries can turn a short overload into a metastable failure that outlasts its trigger. Give retries a budget and drop work nobody waits for; backoff alone only spreads them out.
Changes made by people cause most outages. Fix the system that let the mistake through, practise failures on purpose, and write blameless post-mortems.
The limit: every defence here guards against faults someone thought of. A gray failure or a new kind of bug can still slip past, which is why teams keep practising.

explain.prompt: The person running a small payments company says: "We keep three copies of everything, so we're safe." Explain what three copies protect against, and what they don't.
explain.answer: Three copies protect against faults that strike one part at a time: a disk, a computer, or a whole building if the copies sit in different zones. Losing all three copies to separate hardware failures within one repair window is extremely rare, as long as repairs are quick. They don't protect against faults that hit all three at once, and those cause the big outages. A bug or a bad settings file sent to every copy breaks every copy. Wrong data written to one copy is faithfully passed to the others. And a retry storm overloads all three together. Copies also don't help if the health checks can't see a gray failure, or if switching to a copy has never been tested. So alongside the copies we need changes rolled out in stages, checks on what each program receives, tested error handlers, limits on retries, backups that a bad write can't overwrite, and practice at switching over.

deeper.html:
The 2025 incidents in more detail. At Google Cloud, the blank settings were written to Spanner, Google's worldwide database, and reached Service Control, the part that checks whether each request is allowed. A code path added on 29 May had no error handling and no feature flag, so a null value crashed the program everywhere. A kill switch stopped it, but the status page that should have told customers ran on the broken systems and couldn't be updated at first. At AWS, the race left the DNS record for dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com empty. (DNS, the internet's address book, turns a name into server addresses; the Computer networking track covers it.) DynamoDB errors lasted until 2:40 AM Pacific time, while launching new virtual machines kept failing until 1:50 PM. At Cloudflare, the query that went wrong ran on ClickHouse, a database built for analysis, and the file it produced roughly doubled in size. The file was rebuilt every 5 minutes, so the network kept failing and recovering until the old file was put back at 14:30 UTC. It was not an attack.

Older correlated faults. On 30 June 2012, one extra second, a leap second, was added to the world's clocks. A bug in Linux, the operating system that runs most of the computers behind websites, made many Java programs hang all over the world at once. And some solid-state drives sold by HPE, a big maker of servers, had a bug in their built-in software that made them fail after exactly 32,768 hours of running. Drives put in together died together, which is the correlated fault of the third section hiding inside hardware.

Retries multiply across layers. A request often passes through several layers of code, and each may retry on its own. A library that retries 3 times, called by your code that retries 3 times, behind a network layer that retries 3 times, can turn one request into 27 attempts. Retry at one layer only, and only requests that are safe to repeat. gRPC, a popular library programs use to call each other, builds a retry budget into its clients (retryThrottling). A circuit breaker in a client goes further: after many failures in a row, it stops calling the struggling program for a while, instead of piling on.

Counting at scale. In the second quarter of 2026, Backblaze's fleet saw 1,498 drive failures in 91 days, about 16 a day. The rate is lower than the 2% to 5% a year that studies from 2007 found, which is why older books say a 10,000-disk cluster loses about one disk a day. It's still routine.

Shrinking the repair window. Amazon Aurora's storage keeps 6 copies of the data across 3 availability zones, 2 in each. It needs 4 of them to agree for a write and 3 for a read, which survives losing a whole zone plus one more copy. To make a second fault during a repair unlikely, it cuts the data into 10 GB pieces, so one piece can be re-copied in about 10 seconds over a 10 Gbps link. That is the lab's formula at work: shrink R, and the chance of overlapping failures shrinks with it (Verbitski et al., SIGMOD 2017).

More redundancy can hurt. The gray-failure paper has a surprising case. In a datacenter network with many central switches (the boxes that pass messages between computers), each request passes through more of them as it fans out. So adding switches raises the chance that some request hits the one switch that is silently dropping messages. Redundancy helps against clean failures, and can spread gray ones.

The ironies of automation. Lisanne Bainbridge pointed out in 1983 that automation takes over the easy cases and leaves people the hardest ones, with less practice at them. The S3 outage fits: the restart that took hours was one nobody had needed in years. Chaos engineering and game days, rehearsals of failure on purpose, are partly an answer to that.

The split into hardware faults, software faults and human operations follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 2; the numbers here are newer than the book's.
